strengths: Addresses a practical NLP question: how much annotation makes small specialized models competitive with larger frozen models. Sweeping training sizes from 10 examples to full datasets provides useful information beyond isolated few-shot comparisons.

Most configurations use 100 repetitions and report both mean macro-F1 and standard deviation. The learning curves reveal meaningful differences across datasets, including BERT's failure to overtake the alternatives on BoolQ.

The appendices document model identifiers, prompts, decoding settings, and training hyperparameters, and provide a code link. The limitations candidly describe restricted task coverage and reduced ChatGPT evaluation.
weaknesses: Evaluation independence is unresolved. Section 3 repartitions all labelled data, risking overlap between related SST-2 phrases across training and testing. Flan-T5's prior instruction tuning includes GLUE/SuperGLUE tasks, so original training examples placed in the new test sets also raise contamination concerns. An overlap audit and independent evaluation are necessary to interpret the 'only 10 labels' result.

The BoolQ prompt in Table 1 asks whether the passage contains an answer, whereas BoolQ requires answering the question yes or no. These are different tasks. This mismatch can weaken prompting baselines and distort conclusions attributed to task complexity; the affected experiments need a corrected prompt.

Model selection and annotation accounting are insufficiently specified. The limitations describe selecting prompts using 1,000 training and test examples, while Appendix B invokes early stopping without identifying an independent validation set. This risks test-informed selection and leaves additional supervision uncounted in the reported low-label budgets.

Dataset size is confounded with optimization and actual data consumption. Instruction tuning uses 150 steps with batch size four, processing at most 600 example presentations even for much larger nominal datasets, while encoder training steps increase with dataset size. ICL receives only two to four randomly selected demonstrations. Consequently, the flat curves do not isolate the effect of additional labelled data; convergence checks and clearer separation of available versus consumed labels are needed.

The variance-aware break-even analysis is not statistically calibrated. Although Appendix C acknowledges exceptions, its 'always better' category relies on overlap of mean-plus/minus-standard-deviation bands, which does not establish a specified probability of superiority. Different test-set sizes introduce unequal evaluation noise, and only six ChatGPT repetitions leave its variability poorly estimated. Paired comparisons on common evaluation examples and uncertainty estimates for crossover sizes would better support the central robustness claim.

Quantitative inconsistencies require checking. Figure 2 places an undefined 'Random Baseline' around 60–70 macro-F1, inconsistent with standard random binary predictions. Appendix C describes an increase from roughly 900 to 1,200 labels as 140%, although it is approximately 33%; Table 2 reports 1,750 examples as 35% of a roughly 10,000-example BoolQ training set instead of 17.5%. These discrepancies affect confidence in the numerical recommendations.

The broader conclusions exceed the evidence from three English binary datasets. Task complexity is asserted rather than independently measured, and several competitive ICL comparisons require 3,000–6,000 labels, qualifying the emphasized 100–1,000 range. The practical contribution is promising, but the evaluation and analysis issues require correction and targeted reruns before a sound Findings recommendation.
